title: The Sphinx and the Banknote: Merson from the Old Twelfth to the Vault of Montmartre
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Paris, the birth in the old twelfth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: Day and month attested (fr.wikipedia); the coordinate is reconstructed. The arrondissement the sources give is the pre-1860 twelfth, which covered the Panthéon and Jardin des Plantes quarter, that is, today's fifth, and not the modern twelfth out at Bercy. No birth address was located.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of May a son is born in the twelfth arrondissement of Paris, and in 1846 that name means the Left Bank: the Panthéon on its hill, the Jardin des Plantes, the streets of the old Latin quarter. The numbering will change in 1860 and carry the name away east to Bercy, but the ground of his birth stays where it is. Luc-Olivier Merson will spend nearly the whole of his seventy-four years within a walk of it. He dies in the fifth arrondissement, which is what this quarter becomes, and he keeps his studio on the boulevard Saint-Michel.
suggested_refs: The pre-1860 arrondissements of Paris, in which the twelfth is the Panthéon quarter
sources: fr.wikipedia category, 'Naissance dans le 12e arrondissement de Paris'

stops.name: Paris, the drawing school nobody can name
stops.date_confidence: No source gives any date for this schooling; 1858 is a placement inferred from his age and his later Beaux-Arts entry, not a finding. French Wikipedia names no school at all, appending a maintenance tag that declares the identity unknown. An earlier draft's 'École gratuite de dessin, c.1858-1862' is a guess and is withdrawn.
stops.campa: Before the Beaux-Arts there is a drawing school, and a master named Gustave Adolphe Chassevent-Bacque who teaches the boy to hold a pencil and see an edge. This is the first rung of the ladder every French painter of the century climbs. Which school it was, no source will say. The encyclopedias record the master and then stop, flagging their own ignorance of the building; the coordinate here is a Left Bank placeholder and nothing more. The rung is marked without knowing the address, because the rung is real and the address is lost.
suggested_refs: The municipal drawing schools of Paris under the Second Empire, first training of most Beaux-Arts entrants

stops.name: Paris, the École des Beaux-Arts and Isidore Pils
stops.date_confidence: Entry year not attested by any source; c.1862 is inferred backwards from the 1866 Salon debut. The teacher is attested by both encyclopedias. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from lionel_royer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He enters the school on the rue Bonaparte and puts himself under Isidore Pils, a painter of soldiers and religious subjects who teaches the full academic discipline: the antique cast, the living model, the composed history picture with its arithmetic of gesture. Merson learns it completely. It is the same courtyard and the same plaster casts where Lionel Royer will arrive nine years later, out of the wreck of the war of 1870, to study under Cabanel and Bouguereau. The two of them will spend the rest of their lives painting the same century's subjects.
suggested_refs: The atelier of Isidore Pils at the École des Beaux-Arts, 14 rue Bonaparte

stops.name: Paris, the first Salon in the Palais de l'Industrie
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr. and en.wikipedia); no month or day given, and the work shown is named in no source consulted. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from lionel_royer.journey.json.
stops.campa: At twenty he hangs for the first time in the great glass-and-iron shed on the Champs-Élysées, the hall that holds the annual Salon until the 1890s. Which picture it was, the sources do not record. What matters is the door: from here the Salon is the whole weather of his working life, the place where reputations are made in a fortnight and lost in a season, where the State still runs the jury and a first-class medal is a career. He will hang in this building, and in the halls that replace it, for more than fifty years.
suggested_refs: The Palais de l'Industrie on the Champs-Élysées, home of the Salon until the 1890s

stops.name: Paris, the Institut and the premier grand prix de Rome
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr.wikipedia); the exact date of the award is not recorded in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Under the dome on the quai de Conti the Académie announces the premier grand prix de Rome in painting, and the name is Merson, for a canvas of the soldier of Marathon running himself to death with the news. The prize is signed off under the superintendent Émilien de Nieuwerkerke. It carries a pensionnaire's place at the French Academy in Rome and it is the highest thing a young French painter can be handed. Lionel Royer will compete for it thirteen years later and take only the second prize, which carries nothing at all.
suggested_refs: Le Soldat de Marathon, premier grand prix de Rome, 1869
The Institut de France, 23 quai de Conti

segments.name: Italy, Which the Sources Barely Confirm

stops.name: Rome, the Villa Médicis and Hébert's parting words
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. English Wikipedia gives only 'the five years spent working in Italy'. French Wikipedia's Merson article mentions neither Rome nor the Villa Médicis nor any dates; the residency is inferred from the Prix de Rome, and the range 1870-1874 that circulates is attributed to no source. Coordinate corrected from a draft that used generic Rome city centre.
stops.campa: The prize sends its laureates to the villa above the Spanish Steps, and Merson goes with them: five years in Italy, on the only authority that says anything at all about it. The director's household is Ernest Hébert's, and the young men remember how he dismissed them from an audience. Go, gentlemen, and make nothing but the exquisite. Merson hears it as a laureate of twenty-three. Fifty years later, at a banquet in Paris, a friend will quote the line back at him as the sentence his whole career obeyed.
stops.quote: Allez, Messieurs, et ne faites que de l'exquis
stops.quote_source: Ernest Hébert to his pensionnaires at the Villa Médicis, reported in Paul-Albert-Jean Dagnan-Bouveret's banquet toast to Merson, 23 June 1920, printed in Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (Paris, 1921), pp. 12-13
suggested_refs: The Villa Médicis, seat of the Académie de France à Rome
Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (Paris, 1921), the Dagnan-Bouveret toast
sources: Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (École Nationale des Beaux-Arts, Paris, 1921), pp. 12-13

stops.name: Naples, the museum of the buried towns
stops.date_confidence: Wholly reconstructed. No document places Merson in Naples; the date is a placement inside the presumed Roman years and is not evidence of anything.
stops.campa: Pensionnaires of the French Academy go south. It is part of what the years in Rome are for: the bronzes and the wall paintings lifted out of the buried towns and shelved in the great museum at Naples, the Greek vases, the sculpture the Bourbons collected. Merson is presumed among them, in the way the whole itinerary of his Italian years is presumed. No letter, no register, no signature in a visitors' book has been found to put him personally in this room. The pin marks the custom, not the man.
suggested_refs: The Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Napoli, standard study stop of the Rome pensionnaires
sources: Reconstruction from the standard Prix de Rome pensionnaire itinerary of the 1870s; no Merson-specific document located

stops.name: Pompeii, the forum under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: Wholly reconstructed. No Merson-specific confirmation of a Pompeii visit was located in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The excavated forum with Vesuvius standing over it is the near-obligatory second stop of the southern tour, and every French painter of the period who spends a season in Rome comes back with drawings of it. Merson's Italian years should contain this ground. Nothing found in the sources says they do. What is certain is only what the pictures later show: he acquires somewhere a taste for ruined architecture inhabited by small figures, for broken stone that has outlasted whoever built it, and he will use it for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The forum of Pompeii, excavated and open to visitors through the 1870s
sources: Reconstruction from the standard Prix de Rome pensionnaire itinerary; no Merson-specific document located

stops.name: Assisi, the basilica of Saint Francis
stops.date_confidence: Wholly reconstructed. No source places Merson at Assisi. Coordinate corrected from an earlier draft that fell roughly 800 m southwest of the basilica, outside the church complex.
stops.campa: Up the hill from the Umbrian plain, the double church of San Francesco holds the Giotto cycle that pensionnaires are sent to copy. Whether Merson climbs to it cannot be shown. What can be shown is that four years after Italy he paints the wolf of Gubbio, the beast Francis tamed and made a citizen of a town twenty miles from this door. A painter reaches for that legend from somewhere. The door is recorded here, and it is admitted that no source shows whether he ever walked through it.
suggested_refs: The Giotto cycle of the Life of Saint Francis, Basilica di San Francesco, Assisi
sources: Reconstruction from the standard Prix de Rome pensionnaire itinerary; no Merson-specific document located

stops.name: Florence, the Uffizi corridors
stops.date_confidence: Wholly reconstructed. A Florentine study stop was standard for Rome pensionnaires; nothing whatever documents Merson's.
stops.campa: The Uffizi corridors are the other half of the pensionnaire's education, the Renaissance masters copied hand over hand until the young man's own manner is built out of theirs. Merson's finished style is a bright, hard, evenly lit thing with clean contours and a horror of the smudged, which is roughly what the fifteenth century looks like to the nineteenth. Florence is pinned for that reason and for no better one. There is no document. The presumption is stated plainly rather than dressed up as a finding.
suggested_refs: The Uffizi, copied by generations of French pensionnaires on the northern leg of the Italian years
sources: Reconstruction from the standard Prix de Rome pensionnaire itinerary; no Merson-specific document located

stops.name: Paris, the Salon of 1875 and the first-class medal
stops.date_confidence: Year attested. French Wikipedia calls the medal a Société des artistes français award, which is impossible: that Société was founded only in 1881, after Jules Ferry's request of 27 December 1880, and took the Salon over from the State then. Two French Wikipedia articles contradict each other and the conflict is left open.
stops.campa: Back from Italy he takes a first-class medal at the Salon, the first serious honour of his working life. His last Rome envoi hangs there too, a large composition out of Horace, the wars that mothers hate, made out of the disaster of 1870 which he sat out in Italy while France was invaded. His biographer records the title and the reason. The encyclopedias want to credit the medal to the Société des artistes français; that body will not exist for another six years, and in 1875 the Salon is still the State's.
stops.quote: Son envoi de dernière année fut cette « Bella matribus detestata », vaste composition inspirée par le désastre de 1870
stops.quote_source: Adolphe Giraldon, Luc Olivier Merson: une noble vie d'artiste (Paris, 1929), p. 12. The archive.org scan reads '8on' for 'Son', an OCR substitution recurring elsewhere in the same scan; the transcription is corrected here.
suggested_refs: Bella matribus detestata, the Rome envoi of the final year, Salon of 1875
fr.wikipedia, 'Société des artistes français', founded 1881
sources: Adolphe Giraldon, Luc Olivier Merson: une noble vie d'artiste (1929), p. 12

stops.name: Riom, Saint Michel and the dragon
stops.date_confidence: French Wikipedia dates the canvas 1875 and places it in the musée Mandet at Riom, but never says it was the Salon exhibit or the medal-winning work. An earlier draft made that link; it is unsourced and is withdrawn here.
stops.campa: The archangel stands on the dragon with his sword down, and the canvas goes eventually to the musée Mandet in the little parlement town of Riom in the Auvergne. It carries the same year as the medal, which has tempted more than one writer into saying it won the medal. No source says so. Merson is at this point a religious painter by preference and by market: saints, angels, the Holy Family, the legends of the Franciscans, painted with an archaeologist's finish for a Republic that is busy becoming anticlerical.
suggested_refs: Saint Michel terrassant le dragon (1875), musée Mandet, Riom

stops.name: Paris, the studio and the wolf of Gubbio
stops.date_confidence: Catalogue dates attested (fr.wikipedia): Le Loup d'Agubbio 1877, Saint Isidore le laboureur 1878. The studio address at 115 boulevard Saint-Michel is documented by a photograph caption but carries no date of its own; an earlier draft used a placeholder some 700 m north.
stops.campa: At 115 boulevard Saint-Michel he works in a high room a few streets from where he was born. Out of it in 1877 comes the wolf of Gubbio, the man-eater Francis met on the road and bound by contract to the town, painted as a scene of civic negotiation with the beast sitting patient among the citizens. The next year comes Saint Isidore, the ploughman whose furrow the angels finished while he prayed. Merson paints work and animals and the ordinary miraculous, at a scale meant for the wall of a public building.
suggested_refs: Le Loup d'Agubbio (1877)
Saint Isidore, le laboureur (1878)
The photograph of Merson in his studio at 115 boulevard Saint-Michel
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Luc-Olivier Merson' (catalogue listing and studio photograph caption)

stops.name: Paris, the sphinx in the studio
stops.date_confidence: 1879 attested: exhibited at the Salon of May 1879 under the catalogue title Le Repos en Égypte. The 1880 date that also circulates belongs to a different and larger canvas, not to this one; the long-repeated encyclopedia disagreement dissolves once the two objects are separated.
stops.campa: The picture that outlives everything else he does is made in this room. The Holy Family stops for the night in the desert, and Mary and the child sleep in the lap of a ruined sphinx while Joseph lies on the sand and the moon comes up behind them. It hangs at the Salon in May 1879 as Le Repos en Égypte, seventy-two centimetres by a hundred and twenty-eight. He builds the desert out of prints and lamplight. No record found anywhere places Luc-Olivier Merson in Egypt, at any point, ever.
suggested_refs: Le Repos en Égypte, Salon of May 1879, Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, inv. 18.652
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Le Repos pendant la fuite en Égypte'

stops.name: Cairo, Abu Serga, the refuge he paints and never sees
stops.date_confidence: The date is the painting's, not a visit's. This pin marks the subject and is inherited byte-identical from jesus.journey.json. There is no evidence Merson was ever in Egypt, and that absence is stated as a gap rather than inferred into a finding.
stops.campa: Coptic tradition puts the Holy Family's shelter here, in the crypt under Abu Serga in Old Cairo, the pin inherited from the journey of Jesus himself. Merson paints the same night from four thousand kilometres away, and moves it out of the crypt into the open desert and the lap of a pharaonic monument, so that the new god sleeps inside the head of an old one. The invention is the whole picture. It is also the only reason a French academic painter's route touches Egypt at all.
suggested_refs: Church of St Sergius and Bacchus (Abu Serga), Coptic Cairo, the crypt of the Holy Family
sources: jesus.journey.json (stop: 'Cairo, Abu Serga, the Holy Family in Egypt')
fr.wikipedia, 'Le Repos pendant la fuite en Égypte'

stops.name: Nice, the second version
stops.date_confidence: 1880 attested for this canvas (fr.wikipedia's dedicated article on the painting). It is a variant, 77 x 133 cm, not the Salon picture. No acquisition date for the Saint-Aignan bequest was located.
stops.campa: He paints it again, larger, and this time Joseph does not sleep. He lies awake and looks at the Virgin. The variant goes to the musée des Beaux-Arts de Nice by the bequest of Monsieur de Saint-Aignan; further studies and a version with the whole composition reversed end up at Cleveland. Two encyclopedias spent years disagreeing about whether the painting is from 1879 or 1880. They were describing different objects. A picture this successful gets made more than once, which is how the nineteenth century worked.
suggested_refs: Le Repos pendant la fuite en Égypte (1880), musée des Beaux-Arts de Nice, bequest of M. de Saint-Aignan
The inverted-composition version and studies at the Cleveland Museum of Art
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Le Repos pendant la fuite en Égypte'

stops.name: Paris, the Palais de Salm, chevalier of the Legion of Honour
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr. and en.wikipedia); no date within the year is given. An earlier draft placed all three grades at the Institut de France, which has nothing to do with the order; the Grande Chancellerie is the Palais de Salm, 64 rue de Lille.
stops.campa: The first of three grades. He is thirty-five, medalled, hung every year, and now decorated by the Republic whose subject matter he mostly ignores. The chancellery sits in the Palais de Salm behind the quai Anatole-France, and the ribbon it issues is the exact measure of an official career: chevalier now, officier in 1900, commandeur in the year he dies. Merson will collect the full set. Very few painters of his generation do, and none of them are the ones the twentieth century decides to remember.
suggested_refs: The Palais de Salm, Grande Chancellerie de la Légion d'honneur

stops.name: New York, the window for the Petit Château
stops.date_confidence: 1882 attested (fr.wikipedia) for the execution of the window. Coordinate corrected: an earlier draft used City Hall Park, some 5.6 km from Fifth Avenue at 52nd Street. There is no evidence Merson crossed the Atlantic. The encyclopedias give 1926 and 1927 for the house's demolition; both are printed, neither preferred.
stops.campa: William K. Vanderbilt builds himself a French château at 660 Fifth Avenue and wants French glass in it. Merson draws the design; the atelier of Eugène-Stanislas Oudinot cuts and fires it in Paris and ships it across. The house stands for forty-odd years and comes down in the 1920s, the encyclopedias disagreeing by a year about when. The window leaves Paris; there is nothing to say the designer does. This is the first of the American pins, and every one of them marks where his drawing went.
suggested_refs: The Petit Château, 660 Fifth Avenue, William K. Vanderbilt residence, demolished in the 1920s
The atelier of Eugène-Stanislas Oudinot, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the betrothal dance in glass
stops.date_confidence: 1885 attested for the triptych (fr.wikipedia catalogue listing). No location is given for the design work; the studio pin is a placement, not a finding.
stops.campa: A stained-glass triptych, La Danse des Fiançailles. By the middle 1880s Merson is no longer only a Salon painter: he is a designer whose drawings are executed by other trades in other materials, glass and mosaic and later steel plate and paper. The hand that finishes the object is somebody else's. He works in cartoon, at full size, in the knowledge that a glazier will read it and turn it into lead and pot-metal. It is a medieval way of working, revived, and it suits a man whose subjects are mostly medieval too.
suggested_refs: La Danse des Fiançailles (1885), stained-glass triptych

stops.name: Newport, the Belmont Chapel in the Island Cemetery
stops.date_confidence: 1890 attested (fr.wikipedia). Coordinate corrected from an earlier draft that used downtown Newport, roughly 500 m southwest of the Island Cemetery. No evidence places Merson in Rhode Island.
stops.campa: In the Island Cemetery at Newport the Belmont family raises a memorial chapel, and its chancel windows are Merson's design, executed again by Oudinot's atelier. Three windows in the nave are executed by Félix Gaudin, who takes the workshop over from Oudinot in this very year. The American money of the Gilded Age buys French religious art by the crate, and a Paris draughtsman who has never seen Narragansett Bay furnishes the light that falls on a family's dead. He is paid, the glass is shipped, and he stays on the boulevard Saint-Michel.
suggested_refs: The Belmont Chapel (1890), Island Cemetery, Newport, Rhode Island
The atelier of Félix Gaudin, successor to Oudinot from 1890

stops.name: Biarritz, the window at Sainte-Eugénie
stops.date_confidence: The window's presence is attested (fr.wikipedia); no date whatever is given for it in any source. The year shown is a placement beside the other Oudinot-atelier work and is not a finding. Whether Merson travelled to the Basque coast is unknown.
stops.campa: On the Atlantic coast where the Empress Eugénie made a resort out of a whaling village, the church that carries her name holds a window by Merson. That much the record says. Whether he came down to see the wall it was cut for, or whether the crate went south from the Paris workshop with instructions and he never left the Left Bank, nobody has written down. The glass is pinned. The man is not, because on this one nobody knows where he was. It is the New York problem again, in French.
suggested_refs: Église Sainte-Eugénie, Biarritz, and its Merson window

stops.name: Paris, the gold medal on the Champ de Mars
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr. and en.wikipedia); no date within the year. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from lionel_royer.journey.json.
stops.campa: The Exposition Universelle of 1889 fills the Champ de Mars under a new tower of iron that a good many of the painters of France have signed a letter against. Merson takes the gold medal for painting. The century is showing itself its own machinery, and inside the fine arts pavilion the official school is at its high-water mark: enormous canvases, faultless drawing, subjects out of scripture and legend and the national past, the last decade before that certainty starts to crack.
suggested_refs: The fine arts pavilion of the Exposition Universelle of 1889, Champ de Mars

stops.name: Paris, Notre-Dame and the Hugo commission
stops.date_confidence: The illustration of Hugo's Notre-Dame de Paris is attested (fr.wikipedia); no edition year, print run, or commission date was located, and the year shown is a placement. Whether Merson studied the building on site rather than from prints and photographs is a reconstruction.
stops.campa: He illustrates an edition of Notre-Dame de Paris, and separately the Trophées of José-Maria de Heredia, and draws for La Mosaïque and the Revue illustrée. The cathedral is a twenty-minute walk from his studio and the presumption is that he went and looked. No source records the visit. What the sources do record is the taste: Hugo's Gothic, Heredia's archaeological sonnets, a whole late-century appetite for the exactly reconstructed past, which is the appetite Merson spends his working life feeding.
suggested_refs: Merson's illustrations to Victor Hugo, Notre-Dame de Paris
Merson's illustrations to José-Maria de Heredia, Les Trophées

stops.name: Paris, the Hôtel de Ville
stops.date_confidence: The murals are attested (fr.wikipedia); no commission date was found in any source, and the year shown is a placement inside his decorative decade rather than evidence. Coordinate is the corpus's recurring central Paris pin.
stops.campa: The city hall burned in the Commune fires of 1871 and was rebuilt on its own footprint, and the Third Republic filled it with painting: dozens of artists, hundreds of metres of allegory, a programme of civic virtues for the building where the city governs itself. Merson contributes. Which room, which subject, and which year, the record does not say. This is what the middle of his career looks like from outside: a name on a long list of decorators, in buildings most Parisians walk through without looking up.
suggested_refs: The decorative campaign of the rebuilt Hôtel de Ville de Paris

stops.name: Paris, the Académie Vitti on the boulevard du Montparnasse
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, left open. English Wikipedia gives 1903. French Wikipedia's own Merson article records Marguerite Delorme studying under him at the Académie Vitti from 1890 to 1895, so he was teaching there in the early 1890s. Both readings stand; the street address is itself approximate.
stops.campa: Across the river from the official school, the private academies take the students the Beaux-Arts will not: foreigners, women, anyone with the fee. The Académie Vitti opens in 1889 and Merson teaches there. Marguerite Delorme is in his class from 1890 to 1895; one encyclopedia will later date his teaching to 1903, and both are probably true at their own ends. The academy closes in 1914. He is at once the establishment's man and a jobbing teacher in a Montparnasse room, which is what most establishment careers actually contain.
suggested_refs: The Académie Vitti, 49 boulevard du Montparnasse, 1889-1914
Marguerite Delorme (1876-1946), Merson's pupil there 1890-1895

stops.name: Paris, the Institut, fauteuil 1
stops.date_confidence: Year and seat attested (fr.wikipedia); no date within the year is given.
stops.campa: Twenty-three years after the dome announced his Prix de Rome he is elected under it, to the Académie des beaux-arts, seat number one. From here he sits on juries, on the councils that award the prizes he once won, and on the committees that decide which painters get the walls of public buildings. The academic system is a closed circuit and he is now near its centre. Outside it, in the same city, the dealers on the rue Laffitte are selling the pictures that will make his kind of painting unsellable.
suggested_refs: Fauteuil 1 of the Académie des beaux-arts, Institut de France

stops.name: Carantec, the summers on the Bay of Morlaix
stops.date_confidence: Recurring, not a single event. French Wikipedia gives the summers as 1890s onward with no start or end year; the date shown is a placement in the middle of that fog. The Fransic estate's own coordinates are unknown and the town centre stands in for them.
stops.campa: He is fond of the bay, and the family takes its summers at the Fransic estate at Carantec on the north Finistère coast, in the company of the composer Gabriel Pierné's household. Tide, granite, the oyster beds, the light that has been drawing painters to Brittany for thirty years by the time he arrives. It is the one place outside Paris in the whole documented life where Luc-Olivier Merson is reliably reported to have been, repeatedly, for pleasure, and nobody has recorded which house it was.
suggested_refs: The Fransic estate at Carantec, Baie de Morlaix
The household of the composer Gabriel Pierné

stops.name: Paris, the Palais de Justice
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Only English Wikipedia carries this commission, and it gives no date whatever; French Wikipedia does not mention it. The year shown is a placement.
stops.campa: On the Île de la Cité, in the law courts built around the old royal palace and the Sainte-Chapelle, Merson carries out a decorative commission. One encyclopedia says so and the other is silent, which is the ordinary evidential weather for this part of his life. No subject, no room, no year is recorded. The Palais de Justice is where the Republic keeps its own image of itself as judgment, and the academic painters furnish that image by the metre, on commission, anonymously to everyone who walks past it.
suggested_refs: The Palais de Justice, Île de la Cité, and its late nineteenth-century decorative campaign

stops.name: Paris, the Salle Favart
stops.date_confidence: The mural paintings are attested by French Wikipedia only; an earlier draft also cited English Wikipedia, which does not mention the Opéra-Comique at all. Neither source gives a date. The c.1898 that circulated was reasoned backwards from the 1887 fire and is withdrawn; the year shown is an undated placement.
stops.campa: The Opéra-Comique burned in 1887 with heavy loss of life and was rebuilt as the third Salle Favart. Merson paints murals in it. That single line in a French catalogue listing is the whole of what is known: no subject, no dimensions, no year, no photograph traced. He is by now the sort of artist a public building calls when it needs a ceiling, which is a good living and a kind of invisibility. The work goes up and the name comes off the wall the moment the scaffolding does.
suggested_refs: The third Salle Favart, Opéra-Comique, rebuilt after the fire of 1887

stops.name: Orléans, the entry of the Maid
stops.date_confidence: 1895 attested for the drawing (fr.wikipedia, citing Brême and Korchane, Dessins français du musée des Beaux-Arts d'Orléans, 2022, no. 160). Coordinate corrected: the museum is at 1 rue Fernand Rabier, about 360 m east of the point used in an earlier draft.
stops.campa: Pen and black ink, grey wash, white gouache on white paper, a sheet forty-four by thirty-one centimetres: Joan of Arc entering Orléans. Her actual route put her at the Burgundy gate on the twenty-ninth of April 1429, the city coming out to meet her. Merson draws it four hundred and sixty-six years later, into a national cult of Joan large enough to fill basilicas and museums alike, decades before the church itself catches up. She is beatified in 1909 and canonised in 1920, the year Merson dies.
suggested_refs: Entrée de Jeanne d'Arc à Orléans (1895), musée des Beaux-Arts d'Orléans
Brême and Korchane, Dessins français du musée des Beaux-Arts d'Orléans. Le Trait et l'Ombre (2022), no. 160

stops.name: Paris, the Panthéon, a mural that could not be found
stops.date_confidence: Contested inside this dossier and left open. One lens of the research asserted a Merson Joan of Arc cycle here, installed 1889-1896; the other searched and found nothing, French Wikipedia's article on the building naming other painters and not him. The date shown belongs to the asserted cycle, not to a confirmed work. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from braille.journey.json.
stops.campa: It is exactly the building he ought to be in. The Panthéon in the 1890s is being filled with Joan of Arc cycles by Puvis de Chavannes and Jean-Paul Laurens, a few hundred metres from where Merson was born, on the subject he is drawing in the same decade. But the research could not confirm a single Merson wall here. The gap is recorded plainly: this is where a mural should be, on the evidence of everything around it, and no source can point to it.
suggested_refs: The Joan of Arc cycles of the Panthéon by Puvis de Chavannes and Jean-Paul Laurens
fr.wikipedia, 'Panthéon (Paris)', which does not mention Merson

stops.name: Paris, the Palais de Salm, officier
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr. and en.wikipedia); no date within the year is given.
stops.campa: Nineteen years after the chevalier's ribbon, the second grade. The year is 1900, the year of the great Exposition and the year the Type Merson goes on sale, his own design multiplying itself across the country's mail while the honour is pinned on him in person at the Palais de Salm. Merson is fifty-four, an academician, decorated twice, at the exact height of a system built on faultless drawing and scripture and legend, and for one more year that height still holds.
suggested_refs: The Palais de Salm, Grande Chancellerie de la Légion d'honneur

stops.name: Paris, the Type Merson issued
stops.date_confidence: Issue date attested (fr.wikipedia, 'Type Merson'). An earlier draft's claim that the type stayed in circulation into the 1930s is overstated: the issues run 1900 to 1927 and withdrawal from sale falls in the 1920s.
stops.campa: On the fourth of December the French post issues a new definitive: a seated woman with a branch, the Rights of Man beside her, printed in two colours, the first bicolour stamps France has made. Most of the values are engraved by Auguste Thévenin, in typography, perforated thirteen and a half by fourteen, in sheets of seventy-five. The type runs for twenty-seven years. More people look at this drawing than at every canvas Merson ever painted put together, and almost none of them learn whose it is.
suggested_refs: The Type Merson definitive series, issued 4 December 1900, engraved by Auguste Thévenin

stops.name: Monaco-Ville, the same figure on another state's post
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. English Wikipedia records that Merson designed for the Monégasque administration as well as the French; no year is given, and the date shown is a placement. Nothing suggests he went to Monaco; this pin marks circulation, not travel.
stops.campa: The principality on the rock takes the same designer. A Merson figure goes onto Monégasque postage too, gummed and perforated and licked by people who will never see a Salon. It is the widest his work ever travels and the least of it anyone attributes. The pin is here for what the drawing did, not for what the man did: there is no reason to think Merson ever stood on this rock, and a stamp is not let stand in for a journey. His century is the first in which a line can be in a million pockets while the hand stays on one street.
suggested_refs: Merson designs for the Monégasque postal administration

stops.name: Paris, chef d'atelier on the rue Bonaparte
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, left open. French Wikipedia gives 1905-1911, English Wikipedia 1906-1911. Neither is preferred here. Coordinate inherited byte-identical from lionel_royer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He comes back to the school where Pils taught him, this time as professor and head of an atelier, and he keeps it six years. His colleagues on the teaching council learn a phrase for the moments when his fierce intransigence surfaces in committee. There goes Merson, they say, getting angry. His friend and fellow teacher Adolphe Giraldon writes it down twenty years later, and it is nearly the only thing in two thousand lines of memoir that lets a reader hear the room he was standing in.
stops.quote: Ah! voilà Merson qui se fâche
stops.quote_source: Adolphe Giraldon, Luc Olivier Merson: une noble vie d'artiste (Paris, 1929), p. 45, reporting what colleagues on the École des Beaux-Arts teaching council said of him
suggested_refs: Adolphe Giraldon, Luc Olivier Merson: une noble vie d'artiste (Paris, 1929)
sources: Adolphe Giraldon, Luc Olivier Merson: une noble vie d'artiste (1929), p. 45

stops.name: Paris, the Banque de France and the mark L.O.M 02
stops.date_confidence: Creation date of the 100 francs Luc Olivier Merson attested (fr.wikipedia); circulation from 3 January 1910. An earlier draft called this a 50-franc note put into circulation in 1907; both are wrong, and the 50-franc Merson is a separate note of 1927. Coordinate corrected by about 150 m to 1 rue La Vrillière.
stops.campa: The note created on the second of January is the hundred francs Luc Olivier Merson: Agriculture and Commerce on the face, a seated blacksmith and Fortune with her cornucopia on the back, a hundred and eighty-two millimetres by a hundred and twelve, engraved by Romagnol over a watermark by Frédéric Florian. It is the first polychrome French note actually to circulate. Merson drew it in 1902 and the early printings say so, in a small mark reading L.O.M 02. After lawsuits by his family the mark comes off in May 1909.
suggested_refs: Billet de 100 francs Luc Olivier Merson, created 2 January 1908, circulated from 3 January 1910
The L.O.M 02 mark, removed after 10 May 1909
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Billet de 100 francs Luc Olivier Merson'

stops.name: Paris, Montmartre, the design for the apse
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, left open. French Wikipedia's article on the basilica gives the mosaic as executed from 1918 to 1922 by the atelier Guilbert-Martin; French Wikipedia's Merson gallery caption gives 1923 and credits collaboration with Henri-Marcel Magne. The design date is nowhere stated; an earlier draft's range of c. early 1900s to 1918 was guesswork and is withdrawn.
stops.campa: On the hill above Paris the white basilica of the Sacred Heart wants a Christ for the vault of its apse, and Merson draws it: Christ in glory with his arms open and his heart shown, France and the saints beneath him, four hundred and seventy-three square metres of it. He does not lay a single tessera. The atelier Guilbert-Martin cuts and sets the glass, working from his cartoon, and Henri-Marcel Magne is named as collaborator. It is the largest thing he will ever make and the least of it his own hand touches.
suggested_refs: Le Christ en gloire, apse mosaic of the Basilique du Sacré-Coeur, 473.78 m2
The atelier Guilbert-Martin, Paris

stops.name: Paris, the banquet of the twenty-third of June
stops.date_confidence: Date attested: the toast is printed with it in the memorial exhibition catalogue of May 1921. The Salon medal of honour it celebrates is carried by French Wikipedia and is treated here as reconstruction, the two sources not being independent of each other.
stops.campa: The Salon gives him its medal of honour for a lifetime, and his colleagues sit him down to a banquet. Paul-Albert-Jean Dagnan-Bouveret rises to speak. He tells Merson his work is beautiful and captivating and personal, that its charm goes right through you; he invents an adjective for the delicious world it makes, mersonien; and he closes by handing him the seventeenth century's highest word for a man, l'honnête homme. Five months later Merson is dead, and the speech is printed in the catalogue of his memorial exhibition.
stops.quote: Car elle est belle et captivante et personnelle, votre oeuvre, et son charme est bien pénétrant !
stops.quote_source: Paul-Albert-Jean Dagnan-Bouveret, banquet toast to Merson, 23 June 1920, printed in Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (École Nationale des Beaux-Arts, Paris, May 1921), p. 11
suggested_refs: Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (École Nationale des Beaux-Arts, Paris, May 1921), pp. 11-14
sources: Exposition de l'oeuvre de Luc Olivier Merson (Paris, 1921), pp. 11-14

stops.name: Paris, the Palais de Salm, commandeur
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (fr. and en.wikipedia); no date within the year, and whether it precedes or follows the June banquet is not recorded anywhere reachable.
stops.campa: The third grade, in the last year. Chevalier at thirty-five, officier at fifty-four, commandeur at seventy-four: the Republic's full ladder, climbed by a man who spent his life painting the Holy Family, Franciscan legends, archangels, and the Maid of Orléans. In the same year Joan is canonised in Rome. Whether the ribbon came before the banquet in June or after it, the record does not say, which is the ordinary condition of nearly every date in this life outside the two a registrar wrote down.
suggested_refs: The three grades of the Légion d'honneur held by Merson: 1881, 1900, 1920

stops.name: Paris, the death in the fifth arrondissement
stops.date_confidence: Full date and arrondissement attested (fr.wikipedia); English Wikipedia gives the year only. No street address was located.
stops.campa: On the thirteenth of November he dies in the fifth arrondissement, aged seventy-four. It is the same quarter he was born in, under a different number: the pre-1860 twelfth became the fifth, and Luc-Olivier Merson's whole life fits inside the renaming of one district of Paris. The mosaic on the hill is not finished. The banknote that will carry his name into a third of a billion pockets has not been drawn. The colleagues who toasted him in June bring out the memorial exhibition the following spring.
suggested_refs: The fifth arrondissement of Paris, formerly the twelfth

stops.name: Paris, Père-Lachaise, division 41
stops.date_confidence: The burial is attested (fr.wikipedia, division 41); the burial date is recorded nowhere reachable, and the day shown is a placement a few days after the death. English Wikipedia confirms Père-Lachaise only through a category tag and gives no division.
stops.campa: He is buried in division forty-one. No epitaph has been transcribed, no photograph of the stone was located, and the tomb's present condition is unknown; a search of the standard grave database returned a server refusal, which is recorded here rather than passed over in silence. He lies among the academicians and playwrights and officials of a century that had just ended without much noticing. A pin can be put on the division; what is written on the marble is not yet known.
suggested_refs: Père-Lachaise Cemetery, division 41

segments.name: What the Hand Did Not Touch

stops.name: Paris, Montmartre, the mosaic finished
stops.date_confidence: The basilica's own French Wikipedia article gives completion in 1922, contradicting the 1923 in French Wikipedia's Merson gallery caption. Both are printed and neither is preferred. If the basilica article is right, execution began about two years before Merson's death rather than after it.
stops.campa: The setters finish. Christ stands in the vault over the high altar with his arms open, and the gold ground catches whatever light comes through the drum, and it is one of the largest mosaics in France. The designer has been dead for either two years or three, depending on which article of the same encyclopedia is consulted. Nobody who kneels under it is told his name. It is the fate of the cartoonist: the drawing survives, at enormous scale, inside somebody else's material.
suggested_refs: The completed apse mosaic of the Basilique du Sacré-Coeur, executed 1918-1922 by the atelier Guilbert-Martin

stops.name: Boston, the sphinx crosses the Atlantic
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Museum of Fine Arts holds the 1879 canvas, inventory 18.652, the gift of George Golding Kennedy; the accession year is stated by no source consulted, and the 1918 shown here is inferred from the inventory number alone.
stops.campa: The picture from the Salon of 1879 ends in Boston, given by George Golding Kennedy, catalogued as 18.652. The 1880 variant is in Nice, the reversed version and the studies are in Cleveland, and for most of a century American reproductions of the Virgin asleep in the sphinx's lap outrun anything Merson did in France. It becomes a Christmas card, a magic-lantern slide, a thing people know without knowing whose it is. His best-known work is best known in a country he never visited.
suggested_refs: Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, inv. 18.652, gift of George Golding Kennedy
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Le Repos pendant la fuite en Égypte'

stops.name: Paris, the fifty francs and the end of signatures
stops.date_confidence: Creation date attested (fr.wikipedia, 'Billet de 50 francs Luc Olivier Merson'); circulation from 3 January 1928, withdrawal beginning 26 January 1942, legal tender ending 4 June 1945. The date of the heirs' suit itself is not recorded in any source consulted.
stops.campa: Seven years after his death the Banque de France creates the fifty francs Luc Olivier Merson, engraved from his design by Romagnol and Ernest Deloche: two putti and a young pensive Mercury on the face, a blacksmith with his hand on an inverted hammer beside Minerva on the back, blue and green, a hundred and seventy millimetres by a hundred and twenty-three. Three hundred and ninety-three million are printed. His heirs sue the bank over the rights, and the bank answers by ceasing to name painters and engravers on French notes at all.
suggested_refs: Billet de 50 francs Luc Olivier Merson, created 11 February 1927, circulated 1928-1945
The Banque de France's abandonment of designer credits on banknotes
sources: fr.wikipedia, 'Billet de 50 francs Luc Olivier Merson'

stops.name: Paris, out of the reference works
stops.date_confidence: No date. The eclipse is attested only as a statement by English Wikipedia, with no date range attached; 1940 is a placement. No account of any later rediscovery, retrospective, or catalogue raisonné was located, and no monument or memorial to Merson himself was found.
stops.campa: The verdict, when it comes, is one sentence long: largely forgotten as a result of the overwhelming popularity of the avant-garde art forms. No monument to Merson himself was found, no statue, no plaque, no retrospective. Lionel Royer dies in 1926 and drops out of the reference works the same way; in 1928 Renée Falconetti's face carries the Maid of Orléans onto film and finishes the job painting had been doing since 1875. The images outlive the painters and lose their names on the way.
suggested_refs: en.wikipedia's one-line account of Merson's eclipse
La Passion de Jeanne d'Arc (1928), Renée Falconetti
